prompt: Assume each channel access costs about 200 µs of fixed overhead (DIFS, backoff, PHY preamble, SIFS, Block Ack), and one 1,500-byte frame takes 17 µs of data airtime at your link rate. With frame aggregation (A-MPDU) of **32** frames per access, roughly what fraction of airtime carries data?

options.explanation: That is the efficiency for a single unaggregated frame (17 / 217). Frame aggregation spreads the fixed cost across many frames.
Correct. 32 × 17 = 544 µs of data per 744 µs access: 544 / 744 ≈ 73%.
That would need the overhead to be tiny compared with the data. 200 µs against 544 µs of data is still a large chunk.
50% would mean data and overhead are equal, around 12 frames per access, not 32.

workedExample:
Efficiency is the share of each channel access spent on data:

```formula
T_data = n t_f = 32 × 17 µs = 544 µs
η = T_data / (T_data + T_oh)
η = 544 / (544 + 200) = 544 / 744
η ≈ 0.73 = 73%
where
T_data: the data airtime per channel access, in microseconds (µs)
n: the number of frames aggregated into one access, 32
t_f: the data airtime of one 1,500-byte frame, 17 µs
η: eta, the airtime efficiency: the fraction of airtime carrying data
T_oh: the fixed overhead per access, 200 µs
µs: microsecond, one millionth of a second
≈: approximately equal to
In words: 32 frames share one 200 µs overhead, so nearly three quarters of the airtime carries data.
```

Compare:

```
frames  data   total  eff
  1      17     217    8%
 32     544     744   73%
 64    1088    1288   84%
```

This supplied model illustrates frame aggregation’s benefit. Real overhead also includes per-MPDU fields, padding, acknowledgments and scheduling details; both PHY rate and frame aggregation matter.
